newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebel chief says Chechnya will be independent.
newsitem.headline: Rebel chief says Chechnya will be independent.

text.p: Chechen separatist chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov, who signed a peace deal with Moscow, declared in a television interview shown on Sunday that his southern region would never agree to be part of Russia.

"No Chechen has ever signed any kind of document saying that Chechnya is a part of Russia and there will never be such a Chechen," Maskhadov told Russian Public Television adding that the region could maintain close ties with Russia.
On August 31 Maskhadov and Russian security chief Alexander Lebed signed a peace deal in the town of Khasavyurt just outside Chechnya which ended 21 months of war.
Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, have died in the conflict launched in December 1994 when Russia sent troops to quell the southern region's independence bid.

Under the deal Russian troops, which have failed to establish control over most of Chechnya, started withdrawing from the region. The rebels agreed to put off for five years a decision on whether Chechnya would become independent.
"Lebed was the first Russian statesman to realise that this war leaves Russia with nothing but shame," Maskhadov said praising his negotiating partner.
President Boris Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, last Thursday ended a sombre silence on the Chechnya question by backing Lebed.
"My aide Alexander Lebed fulfilled my instruction and stopped the military conflict," he said in a radio address.

But Yeltsin and other top politicians, including Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, have stressed that their approval was based on the understanding that the deal was meant to keep Chechnya as part of Russia.
Chernomyrdin reiterated this point of view after a meeting with rebel chief Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev in Moscow on Thursday.
The separatists have made clear they have a different vision of the accord.
Yandarbiyev has said that the deal was struck to give Moscow a face-saving excuse to let Chechnya go rather than a time for the separatists to change their mind.

Lebed has said he was not worried by rebel statements. He has said that five years of peace and realities of life in landlocked Chechnya would make the separatists more willing to reduce their demands to ones for strong autonomy.
But his opponents attacked him in parliament last week saying that the agreement in fact rubber-stamped Chechnya's secession.
Many deputies in the State Duma lower house loudly cheered Lebed's strong opponent, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, when he branded the deal as a "humiliating admission of defeat."

"You need not be too clever to realise that the Khasavyurt agreements were fiction," he told the Duma. "They were a mere cover for unlimited concessions in the most humiliating and devastating forms."
Maskhadov described Kulikov as a key war-monger.

"Kulikov has always been the main obstacle in the way of peace in Chechnya," he said. "He has made a rapid career during this bloody and infamous war, rising to be a minister and full general. Of course Kulikov does not want this war to end."
